Better Place failed in both countries because the company did not fully understand the social, economic, and cultural factors that would have been required to make it a success.

Better Place failed because the company did not understand how its customers interpreted and interacted with its products, and because it did not understand the political and economic contexts in which its products were introduced.

Better Place failed due to a combination of reasons, including that the market for electric vehicles was not as large as expected, that the market was not as “green-friendly” as it seemed, that the company was unable to convince the public that its solution to range anxiety was a real problem, that it was unable to convince consumers that it was a better solution to charging time, that it did not understand the local culture, and that the company did not fully understand the local market and its needs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Better Place model was too complex for the market to adopt, especially when compared to the simplicity of the gasoline and diesel model.

Better Place failed because of a combination of factors, which included the following: (1) the company's failure to recognize the interpretive flexibility of the electric vehicle market; (2) the company's inability to recognize and adapt to the local context of the market in Denmark and Israel; and (3) the company's lack of understanding that its proposed solution addressed a psychological, not functional barrier, to electric vehicle adoption.
the Better Place case shows that electric mobility is still a long way off, and that the current focus on the technology and the infrastructure is misplaced.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the failure of Better place was a failure of the market and not a failure of the technology.
Better Place failed to address the psychological barriers of electric vehicle adoption, and that the “greenness” of a country cannot be taken at face value.
the success of electric vehicles is not a given, and that the public and policymakers should not expect a smooth transition to a low-carbon transportation system.
